headline: US forces struck three Iranian crude oil tankers on Saturday and CENTCOM warned it would if necessary destroy Iran's oil fleet - on the same day AAA's own data recorded an all-time record US diesel average of $5.8819 a gallon. Separately, three hours of Witkoff and Kushner talks with Putin at the Kremlin produced a readout but no breakthrough, and a fragile 72-hour pause on strikes against capitals only. With US markets shut today and Monday for Labor Day, none of it can be priced until Tuesday's open - the same morning Canada's C$27.6bn counter-tariffs take effect.
client_frame_short: If a client asks you one thing this week it will not be about payrolls. It will be **why everything costs more when the news says the economy is strong**. You now have the cleanest possible answer, and it is sitting on AAA's own website. Diesel set an all-time record on Saturday at $5.8819 a gallon, up 58.4% from $3.7123 a year ago. Regular gasoline is $4.1459 against $3.2046 last September, up 29.4%. Meanwhile Friday's jobs report showed average hourly earnings growing just 3.1% year-over-year. That gap - wages up 3%, diesel up 58% - is not a talking point. It is the entire reason the Federal Reserve is discussing raising interest rates in nine days rather than cutting them.
client_frame:
The useful frame for this week is that your clients are about to experience the inflation problem physically, on a holiday weekend, at a fuel pump, and that experience will shape how they hear everything else you tell them. AAA's national average for diesel hit $5.8819 a gallon on Saturday. That is not an estimate or a forecast: AAA's own highest-recorded-price field now reads $5.8819 set 9/5/26, so the record was made this weekend. A year ago diesel averaged $3.7123. That is a 58.4% increase. Regular gasoline is $4.1459 versus $3.2046 last September, up 29.4%, and AAA's own site headline reads Labor Day On Track to Set Record at the Pump. Diesel is the number that matters more than gasoline even though clients notice gasoline first, because diesel moves freight, and freight costs are embedded in the price of everything that arrives on a truck. 

Now set that beside Friday's jobs report. The economy added 162,000 jobs in August against a consensus of 56,000, and the prior two months were revised UP by a combined 55,000 - July actually flipped from a reported loss of 23,000 jobs to a gain of 21,000. By any conventional reading that is a strong report. But average hourly earnings grew only 3.1% year-over-year, DECELERATING from 3.2%, and that is below the 3.4% pace of consumer price inflation in July. So the honest summary is: plenty of jobs, wages growing slower than prices, and the most freight-sensitive fuel in the economy at an all-time high. A client who tells you the economy does not feel as good as the headlines is not being irrational. They are describing real wages correctly. 

This is also the cleanest explanation you will get all year for why the Federal Reserve is being discussed as a candidate to RAISE rates on September 16 rather than cut them. Futures put the odds of a hike at roughly 57% on Friday's cohort, and the probability of a cut at any meeting through March 2027 is exactly zero. Many clients still carry a mental model in which the Fed's next move is downward, because that was the story for most of the last two years. That model is now wrong by direction, and it is worth correcting explicitly rather than letting a client discover it from a headline. The reason is visible at the pump. 

Where this gets genuinely useful for portfolio conversations is the distinction between what the Fed can and cannot fix. Saturday's escalation - US forces striking three Iranian crude tankers, with CENTCOM threatening Iran's wider oil fleet - is a supply-side event. Higher interest rates do not produce more diesel. They work by cooling demand, which is a slow and blunt instrument against a shock originating in the Strait of Hormuz. So if a client asks whether the Fed can do anything about fuel prices, the accurate answer is: not quickly, and not directly. What the Fed is actually defending is the expectation that inflation returns to target, which is why it may raise rates into an energy shock even though that feels counterintuitive. 

The practical counsel for the week is patience about timing rather than any change in allocation. US markets are closed today and closed Monday for Labor Day. Three days of accumulating news - the tanker strikes, an OPEC+ meeting happening this morning, a German state election counting votes this afternoon, and whatever comes out of the envoys' meeting in Kyiv - has no US venue to be priced in until Tuesday morning, and Tuesday is also the morning Canada's counter-tariffs on C$27.6bn of American goods take effect. That is a recipe for a noisy open that will look more dramatic than it is, because it will contain three days of repricing compressed into one session. Then on Friday the August CPI report arrives, which the Fed has effectively named as the deciding input for its September vote. The right posture is to expect the noise, decline to trade it, and remember that a single volatile session in a holiday-shortened week is not information about a long-term plan.
geo_headlines: IRAN / OIL - THE MOST TRADEABLE DEVELOPMENT OF THE WEEKEND. US forces struck three Iranian crude oil tankers on Saturday September 5 after Iran launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships; an aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer evaded the attacks and no US personnel were injured. CENTCOM said it would, if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet. One crude carrier was permanently disabled. The significance is the change of target class: Iran's earlier maritime attacks hit commercial shipping, whereas this is the United States striking Iran's own state export fleet and threatening the rest of it. That is a supply-side escalation rather than a sentiment one, and it happened after Friday's oil settles were struck, so neither the WTI nor the Brent tile above reflects it. Confirmed by AP copy carried at notus.org, by BBC News timestamped 14:35 GMT September 5, and by a Reuters live file. IRGC counter-claims - that it targeted three tankers transiting Hormuz without approval, and struck a US drone boat on September 6 - are single-sourced and unverified.

RECORD DIESEL, PRIMARY SOURCE NOW OBTAINED. AAA's national average for diesel is $5.8819 a gallon on a page priced 9/5/26, and AAA's own highest-recorded-average-price field shows that exact figure set on that exact date - so this is an all-time record by the publisher's own data, set inside this run's window. Regular gasoline is $4.1459, mid-grade $4.6547, premium $5.0376. Year-ago comparisons: diesel $3.7123, up 58.4%; regular $3.2046, up 29.4%. Diesel is up 4.9% in a week and 9.7% in a month. AAA's own site headline reads Labor Day On Track to Set Record at the Pump. This CORRECTS run #173, which carried a secondary-source diesel figure roughly three cents light and flagged it as unverified; the primary is now in hand. Diesel matters more than gasoline for inflation transmission because it prices freight, and freight is embedded in the delivered cost of nearly everything.

KREMLIN MEETING - A READOUT, NOT A BREAKTHROUGH. Putin gave Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner more than three hours at the Kremlin on Saturday; the envoys left around 11 p.m. Moscow time. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks substantive, very frank, and constructive, and said the Americans put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement - without saying what they were. Putin told the pair Russia was making real progress on the battlefield and stressed the need to address all the root causes of the conflict. A White House official said the two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks. That is the language of a process, not a deal. No ceasefire, framework, or agreement was announced by either side, and Reuters' own framing was that Ushakov gave no indication of any breakthrough. The absence of an agreement is itself the readout.

THE ONE CONCRETE DELIVERABLE IS A 72-HOUR PAUSE ON CAPITALS ONLY - DO NOT UPGRADE IT TO A CEASEFIRE. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin ordered Russian forces not to strike Kyiv for three days, and explicitly did not extend that to other parts of Ukraine. Zelensky reciprocated on Telegram at 5:21 p.m. local time Saturday: from the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a halt in aerial strikes on the cities involved in the negotiating process. Both declarations were unilateral, both are tied to the envoys' visit, and neither side has used the word ceasefire. Sources also render the start date differently - one has the order beginning at midnight September 5, another covering September 6 to 8 - and that ambiguity is worth preserving rather than resolving. The war did not stop: Russia flew 108 drones overnight into September 6, of which Ukraine's Air Force reported 88 downed or suppressed, with strikes recorded at 11 locations. Casualty tallies are still moving and credible sources disagree - 7 to 8 killed and 57 to 69 injured across five regions, including an 11-year-old boy in Kharkiv oblast.

THE KYIV LEG IS HAPPENING AS THIS BRIEF PUBLISHES AND HAS NO READOUT - THE LARGEST LIVE HEADLINE RISK ON THIS PAGE. Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Ukraine on September 6, their first visit to the country since taking lead roles on the war file, confirmed by the Kyiv Independent's dated front page and by BBC News timestamped 02:24 GMT. Zelensky said beforehand that he had met Ukraine's negotiating team and that its proposals were ready: we are ready for the conversation, Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive. As of 07:12 ET there is no readout of the meeting itself. Anything reported later today about what was agreed in Kyiv post-dates this brief. Note also that Ukrainian drones reportedly struck Russia's Ryazan oil refinery - consistent with Zelensky's pledge, which covered capitals and not energy infrastructure, and relevant to crude and products if confirmed.

VERIFIED NON-DEVELOPMENT ONE: NO FED, TREASURY, OR TRADE PRINCIPAL SPOKE. No Federal Reserve, Treasury, White House economic, or Commerce official was booked on any Sunday show whose lineup could be verified. The senior economic-adjacent booking of the day is Energy Secretary Chris Wright, on both CBS Face the Nation and ABC This Week - notable in its own right given record diesel and the Iran situation, but his remarks air after 9 a.m. ET and therefore after this publication. The Fed's communications blackout began Saturday September 5 and runs through Thursday September 17, confirmed against the St. Louis Fed's blackout-period schedule, so a Fed appearance would have been extraordinary. Meet the Press, State of the Union, and Fox News Sunday had not published September 6 lineups at research time. A trap worth flagging: a widely circulating clip of Canada's trade minister saying we are not waiting by the phone is dated August 25, not this weekend.

VERIFIED NON-DEVELOPMENT TWO: TRUMP SAID NOTHING NEW. No statement on interest rates, the Federal Reserve, Fed personnel, or trade was found inside the Saturday-to-Sunday window; a searchable Truth Social archive showed no posts dated September 5 or 6. Everything circulating is Friday material being re-reported. For the record, Friday's confirmed post celebrated the jobs number as nearly TRIPLE the predictions of the Bloomberg survey's so-called Economists. A Saturday-datelined CNBC synthesis piece on the pressure campaign against Chair Kevin Warsh describes entirely Friday events, including a new threat to halt trade with surplus countries unless the Fed cuts, and senior economic counselor Peter Navarro calling a hike careless and FOMC members clowns. Warsh is the sitting chair, not a pending appointee, and has said publicly the president has had no impact on his decisions. No Fed Board personnel development this weekend.

OPEC+ IS MEETING AT THIS BRIEF'S PUBLICATION HOUR AND NO DECISION EXISTS YET. Eight core OPEC+ members including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman convened online on Sunday September 6 at approximately 1100 GMT, which is 07:00 ET. Three sources told Reuters ahead of the meeting they were likely to keep October output policy unchanged, with attention shifting to contentious 2027 quota negotiations; September completes the unwinding of one layer of cuts while another remains in place for most of the 21-country group through end-2026. THAT IS A REPORTED EXPECTATION, NOT A DECISION. As of 07:12 ET opec.org carried no September 5 or 6 press release and the Reuters wire mirror carried nothing later than September 4. Any outcome is unpublished at the time of writing, and it lands into a market that cannot trade it until Tuesday.

GERMANY - A REAL TAIL RISK COUNTING VOTES THIS AFTERNOON. Saxony-Anhalt votes today, with initial results expected around 6 p.m. local time, which is 12:00 ET. The far-right AfD under 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund has POLLED just over 40% against 23% for Merz's CDU and could become the first far-right party to hold power at German state level since the Second World War, with a genuine chance of an absolute majority if smaller parties miss the 5% threshold - which would let it bypass the mainstream firewall entirely. THAT 40% IS A POLL, NOT A RESULT, and nothing about the outcome is known as this brief publishes. If the AfD falls short, a CDU-led administration under incumbent premier Sven Schulze is the likelier path. The transmission channel to portfolios runs through Bund spreads, the euro, and European political-risk premium. Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern vote two weeks later.

VERIFIED NON-DEVELOPMENTS THREE THROUGH SIX, EACH CHECKED AND EACH EMPTY. Canada's counter-tariffs on C$27.6bn of US goods remain on track for 12:01 a.m. Tuesday September 8 at rates of 15, 25 and 50 percent; Finance Canada's live product list was last dated September 1 and saw no weekend update, and no negotiation, delay, or carve-out was found. No Chinese data was published - both China Customs and the National Bureau of Statistics show no September 5 or 6 release, so August trade, CPI, PPI and credit are all still ahead. No Bank of Japan or Ministry of Finance official spoke after September 4, when currency chief Atsushi Mimura said there was no change to our stance of being on alert to currency moves. And no weekend crypto catalyst of any kind was found - no regulatory action, no exchange incident, no ETF news - which is why bitcoin traded a range of roughly $476 and needs no explanation beyond noise. Oracle and Adobe both still report after Thursday's close with no weekend news on either. Elsewhere: Anak Krakatau's eruption has suspended flights at Jakarta's main airport with more than 20,000 passengers stranded, with no commodity or shipping impact reported.
